title: Where Will AMD Be in 2028?
detail:
Where Will AMD Be in 2028?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 9:25 AM MST 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) has delivered strong returns this year, but unless you've held over the past 10 months, you haven't gained anything. The bigger risk lies in what's ahead for AMD, as that will determine future returns.

AMD has to continue proving itself to the market quarter after quarter, as there is a lot of skepticism about its positioning compared to other industry giants. By 2028, I think this will be clear, but where will the stock be? I think it will be in the exact same spot. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD's growth has already been pulled ahead

For most of AMD's life, it has always been viewed as an alternative product line, rather than the industry standard. This has hurt it on more than one occasion, and the AI build-out is no different. Nvidia is seen as the industry standard, with AMD as a solid alternative. But it's not the first choice.

However, AMD's products are starting to be used in more applications, and this has caused its data center revenue growth rate to spike. In Q2, its data center revenue rose 107% year over year, so clearly it's starting to become a more popular choice. AMD will need to continue that performance for the foreseeable future, as there is a ton of growth already priced into the stock.

Currently, AMD's shares trade at a very expensive 136 times trailing earnings. To make matters worse, it was over 160 just a few days ago.

AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts

That's a very optimistic price tag, and it indicates there is a lot of expected growth that has been pulled forward. If you value the stock based on 2027 earnings, this is confirmed.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

AMD's stock trades for 33.5 times next year's earnings, not this year's. That's a huge premium, and I think it's a bit absurd. For comparison, the industry standard is Nvidia. It trades at 27 times earnings right now. So, there is well over a year and a half worth of growth already priced into the stock.

By the beginning of 2028, I think AMD's stock will not have budged much. It needs to go through a year or so of lackluster stock growth so that business results can catch up to the stock price. The stock is well in front of the business right now, which can cause poor future returns. If you're sitting on big AMD gains, now may be the time to sell and find a different stock. If you haven't bought any, now probably isn't the best time to get in.

Advanced Micro Devices has been one of the headline AI chip stocks, and after a multiyear surge the real question is whether its current share price lines up with the cash flows the business is expected to produce.

Over the past 3 years the stock has returned very roughly 4.8x, which puts a lot of weight on the idea that future cash generation can support such a step up in equity value.

New AI infrastructure efforts like the Helion rack blueprint and large GPU deployments with partners such as Vultr and Fermi can influence how quickly AMD converts those opportunities into cash, and how much capital it needs to commit along the way.

The issue now is whether AMD's cash flows, as captured in a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) view, are strong enough to justify where the shares trade today.

If you are weighing AMD's 475.4% three year return against the cash flow expectations now priced in, it can help to line it up against other AI infrastructure names using the 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

Is Advanced Micro Devices Still Cheap on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) approach values Advanced Micro Devices based on the cash it is projected to return to shareholders over time. AMD generated about $8.7b of free cash flow over the last twelve months, which gives this model a solid starting point rather than an early stage guess.

The projections assume growing free cash flow over the coming decade, which fits a business investing heavily in AI infrastructure such as Helion racks and large GPU clusters. At a share price of $552.72, the DCF result sits modestly above where the market currently trades the stock. This implies investors are already baking in strong execution but not pushing expectations to extremes. Applied Materials Sinks 7% on Lam's Outlook: "A Bit Higher" Wasn't Enough ©Kuzmik_A from Getty Images Pro and IncrediVFX from Getty Images via Canva

Applied Materials (AMAT:NASDAQ) shares are down about 7.4% today (trading at about $380) after Lam Research (LRCX:NASDAQ) said supply-chain constraints held back its December-quarter outlook.

Applied Materials reported nothing. It's paying for a peer's guidance, even though that peer forecast a sharp jump in chip-equipment spending for 2027.

What Lam Actually Said

Lam posted record September-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion, up 22% from June, and guided December-quarter revenue to $8.6 billion (plus or minus $400 million).

CFO Doug Bettinger said the guide "would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints." (He didn't size it.)

Lam sees 2026 wafer fab equipment (WFE) spending in the mid-$150 billion range, with a preliminary 2027 figure above $200 billion.

Lam shares fell about 9% at the open and ASML (ASML:NASDAQ about 4%, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ), Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ)and Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) also slipped.

Applied's Multiple Has Already Been Cut in Half

Applied Materials traded at 48.94x next-twelve-month earnings at its July peak. It now sits at 23.19x, well under its 30.80x average.

AMAT Stock NTM P/E: 1-Year (TIKR)

That's a 53% de-rating, delivered alongside a record fiscal third quarter. Lam expects to ship December's delayed tools in the March quarter, though it sees constraints lasting into 2027. At 23x, the stock is pricing in more than a delay.

The Number That Has to Hold

The exposure sits in the estimates. Analysts expect Applied's revenue to climb from $34.26 billion in fiscal 2026 to $46.37 billion in fiscal 2027. That's a 35% jump in a year Lam expects industry spending to top $200 billion.

AMAT Revenue Estimates (TIKR)

Applied has planned for this kind of bottleneck. In May, CFO Brice Hill said the company had "nearly doubled our manufacturing capacity" and shares customers' eight-quarter forecasts with suppliers.

Where Applied Materials Stock Goes From Here

The Street hasn't flinched. The mean target was $628 on October 21, barely below September's $639 and about 65% above today's price.

AMAT Stock Mean Price Target: 3-Year (TIKR)

Today looks like the market treating a timing problem as a demand problem. Applied's November 12 report will show whether fiscal 2027 still points toward $46 billion. If it does, 23x is cheap.

The upside depends on three catalysts: the Intel 18A ramp, accelerating Data Center and AI demand, and a foundry business that can win outside customers. If all three deliver, the recent pullback would sit within a real turnaround.

Intel Gave Back 14% in a Month Despite Record Growth

Intel shares have fallen 8.31% over the past week and 14.43% over the past month. Still, the stock is up 151.84% year to date and stands about 34.7% below its 52-week high of $142.35.

On Monday, JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM), a longtime bear, upgraded Intel to neutral from underweight. Intel's third-quarter report is expected after the close on October 29.

The last earnings report was strong. Q2 revenue came in at $16.13 billion (+25.4% YoY), ahead of estimates for $14.45 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.42 exceeded the $0.22 consensus. CEO Lip-Bu Tan called it the "strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years."
